sceneHappening: Zacchaeus in Jericho, the parable of the minas, the entry into Jerusalem, and tears over the city
summary: Jesus enters Jericho and is passing through. A man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector and rich, wants to see who Jesus is, but being short, can't see over the crowd, so he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore fig tree. Jesus looks up and says, "Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house." He hurries down and receives him joyfully, and all grumble, "He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner." Zacchaeus says, "Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much." Jesus says, "Today salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost." Because he is near Jerusalem and they think the Kingdom of God will appear at once, he tells a parable: a nobleman goes into a far country to receive a kingdom and return. He calls ten servants, gives them ten minas, and says, "Conduct business until I come." His citizens hate him and send a delegation after him: "We don't want this man to reign over us." When he returns having received the kingdom, he calls the servants to see what they have gained. The first has made ten more, and the king says, "Well done, you good servant. Because you were found faithful with very little, you shall have authority over ten cities." The second has made five, and is given five cities. Another brings back his mina wrapped in a handkerchief: "I feared you, because you are an exacting man." The king says, "Out of your own mouth will I judge you, you wicked servant," and takes the mina from him and gives it to the one who has ten. "To everyone who has, will more be given; but from him who doesn't have, even that which he has will be taken away." And the king says, "Bring here these enemies of mine, who didn't want me to reign over them, and kill them before me." After saying this he goes ahead, going up to Jerusalem. Near Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sends two disciples to bring a colt that no one has sat on; "If anyone asks you, 'Why are you untying it?' say 'The Lord needs it.'" As he rides, people spread their cloaks on the road, and as he comes down the Mount of Olives the whole multitude of the disciples begin to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen: "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!" Some Pharisees say, "Teacher, rebuke your disciples," and he answers, "I tell you that if these were silent, the stones would cry out." When he sees the city, he weeps over it: "If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For the days will come on you, when your enemies will throw up a barricade against you, surround you, hem you in on every side, and will dash you and your children within you to the ground. They will not leave in you one stone on another, because you didn't know the time of your visitation." He goes into the temple and begins to drive out those who sell, saying, "It is written, 'My house is a house of prayer,' but you have made it a den of robbers." He is teaching daily in the temple, and the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people seek to destroy him, but can't find a way, for all the people hang on his words.
whySettingMatters: Jericho was a rich city, with a customs station on the trade route and balsam and palm groves, so a chief tax collector like Zacchaeus would have been wealthy and hated. Tax collectors collected more than was due for their own profit, which is why Zacchaeus's promise to repay fourfold goes beyond the law's requirement (Exodus 22:1 and Leviticus 6:5 ask for repayment with an added fifth). His name is the Hebrew for "pure" or "righteous." A grown man climbing a tree in public was undignified, and Jesus' invitation to eat at his house, again at the center of grumbling, marks him as someone welcomed. The parable of the minas draws on a known story: after Herod the Great died, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome to be confirmed as king, and a Jewish delegation went after him to oppose it (Josephus). A mina was about one hundred days' wages. The king's reward of cities, the third servant's excuse, and the enemy citizens' judgment each speak to different hearers. The entry into Jerusalem in Luke has the word "king" for the first time and echoes the angels' song at the birth (2:14). "The stones would cry out" recalls Habakkuk 2:11. The weeping over Jerusalem describes a siege with an embankment, a detail that matches Rome's siege in AD 70; whether this was written after the event or is a prophecy is debated. "The time of your visitation" picks up Zechariah's song (1:68, 1:78).

questions: Zacchaeus climbs a tree and then promises restitution. What changed between the two?
Jesus said, "The Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost." What does that verse sum up about Luke's Gospel?
The parable of the minas has a king, servants, and enemies. Where do you see yourself, and what is it asking for?
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as the crowd cheers. What does he see that they don't?
